study.title: Ezekiel 36 Judgment, restoration and sanctification of the name of God
study.overview: Ezekiel 36 unites two complementary messages: God responds to Israel's public shame before the nations and at the same time exposes that the deepest problem of the people was not only territorial, but moral and spiritual. The chapter begins with the promise of reversal of the ruin of the earth, humiliation of enemies and reconstruction of the devastated places. Then the focus shifts to Israel's guilt: the land was contaminated by its ways, and exile made this impurity visible. The promised restoration will not be mere geographical return; God promises to cleanse the people, give new heart, put his Spirit in him and produce real obedience. The ultimate goal is for the nations to recognize who the Lord is, and that the people themselves be ashamed of their sins and live as a renewed people.

outline.title: God reacts to the reproach against the land of Israel
outline.explanation: The mountains, valleys, ruins, and abandoned cities are personified to announce that the LORD has seen the mockery of the nations and will not leave humiliation without answer. The desolation of the enemies, especially of Edom, is presented as a just retribution for the joyful and negligible appropriation of the earth.

outline.title: Fecundity, settlement and end of shame
outline.explanation: The land goes from devastated to fruit: it produces branches, fruit, crops and abundant settlement. The promise includes reconstruction, multiplication of men and animals, the end of the extermination and withdrawal of shame that said the land devoured people.

outline.title: Israel's guilt and the honor of God's name
outline.explanation: God recalls that Israel defiled the land by blood and idols, was scattered among the nations, and there he defiled the name of the LORD. Restoration is not born of the merit of the people, but from the zeal of God by his own name, which he promises to sanctify before the nations.

outline.title: Purification, new heart and restored abundance
outline.explanation: Restoration culminates in purification, inner renewal, and obedience empowered by the Spirit of God. The people return to the land, the famine ceases, the cities are rebuilt, and the land becomes like a fertile garden; all this so that the nations may know that the LORD is the one who rebuilds and replants.

study.context: The chapter addresses the "mountains of Israel," showing that the land and the people are linked in the covenant: the desolation of the territory reflects the divine discipline over the nation. The notes provided relate the immediate context to the opposition of Edom and the neighbouring nations, who rejoiced at the ruin of Israel. The text also resumes the idea of purity and impurity, so important in Ezekiel: the earth was corrupted by blood and idols, and the people need purification so that God will dwell again in between him. The notes also suggest that the external restoration points to a deeper transformation, which goes beyond returning to the ground.
study.theology: Ezekiel 36 teaches that the holiness of God governs both judgment and restoration. Sin is not treated as a light error, but as real contamination that profanes the earth and dishonors the name of the LORD among the nations. At the same time, restoration does not depend on the moral dignity of the people; God acts because of his own name and glory. This prevents any human boasting. The promise of the new heart and the Spirit highlights that true obedience is born of an inner renewal granted by God. Salvation, therefore, is not only external return or social improvement, but a spiritual transformation that produces obedient life. The chapter also points to the missionary dimension of divine action: the nations will recognize who the Lord is when they see their people purified, restored and inhabiting in fidelity.

scholarViews.insight: The restoration of the land is presented as a reversal of the previous devastation: the ruin of the mountains of Israel will be undone after the judgment on Edom and the opposing nations.
The chapter is divided between a promise of temporal restoration of the condition of the people and another of spiritual renewal, showing that God treats both the external and moral state of Israel.
The prophet speaks to the mountains of Israel to comfort the land with the expectation of restoration before the enemies who had wrongly claimed it.

questions: Why does the Lord insist that restoration happens because of his name and not on the merit of Israel?
What changes in someone's life when God promises not only to forgive, but also to give a new heart and his Spirit?
In what ways can the public shame of God's people become an opportunity for God to be known to the nations?
study.practice: This chapter calls the church to abandon all confidence in justice itself and to depend on the grace that purifies and transforms. In practice, this means confessing sins without excuses, asking God to form in us an obedient heart and desire that our lives publish his holiness before others. He also teaches to wait for restoration with humility: God not only repairs circumstances, but renews people. In periods of ruin, the text encourages to pray that the Lord will rebuild what has been destroyed and make his presence recognized through a renewed people.
study.uncertainty: The given notes point out different interpretive readings about the final scope of the chapter: some mainly emphasize the historical return of the people to the earth, while another reading sees a broader fulfillment in redemption in Christ. Since the request requires the basis of the notes only, this synthesis records both directions as interpretations, without declaring one as unique and definitive. There are also not enough details in the given notes to accurately set date, location or specific political circumstances beyond the general mention of enemies and Edom.
